caption: A starry sky over the domes of La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: A dense sweep of bright stars fills the sky above a mountaintop, where a lone human silhouette stands among a couple of large, dark telescope domes. The figure is the photographer himself, astronomer Håkon Dahle, pictured at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

Dahle made these photos during a week of observing at the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope. From time to time the telescope passed to another observing team, which left him free to step outside, enjoy the view and record it for everyone else. Plenty of professional astronomers share this hobby, and ESO's sites in the Atacama Desert are prized for both research and photography.

Seeing the Milky Way at all takes effort for most people. It shines more brightly from the Southern Hemisphere, but it is still faint, and city lights or even the Moon can wash it out. La Silla sits far from urban glare under very clear air, and its skies are dark enough that the Milky Way alone can cast a visible shadow.
explore: The extra brightness of the Milky Way in southern skies comes down to geometry: Earth's southern regions face towards the dense centre of our galaxy. Dahle entered this picture in the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group, which ESO reviews regularly to choose photos for its Picture of the Week series and its gallery.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph taken by astronomer Håkon Dahle; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the star field may look richer here than it would to someone standing on the mountain.

alt: A bright field of stars over a mountaintop, with a silhouetted person standing among dark observatory domes.

caption: Yepun, the VLT's fourth Unit Telescope, under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Lit by the stars of the Milky Way, a large telescope enclosure stands on the summit of Cerro Paranal, poised for a night of observing. This is Yepun, the fourth Unit Telescope (UT4) of ESO's Very Large Telescope, photographed by John Colosimo.

Yepun carries a main mirror 8.2 metres across and is one of four Unit Telescopes that make up the VLT. Its companions are Antu, Kueyen and Melipal. The four names come from the language of the Mapuche people and mean, in turn, Venus, the Sun, the Moon and the Southern Cross. Combined, the four telescopes act as the VLT Interferometer, which lets astronomers pick out details up to 16 times finer than a single telescope can.

Near the plane of the Milky Way, at the heart of Scorpius, shines the red star Antares. Around it the stars are so crowded that most other objects and constellations are hard to make out. The shutter stayed open for 30 seconds, long enough for Earth's rotation to stretch each star into a short trail.
explore: Paranal Observatory sits 2635 metres above sea level and is ESO's flagship facility, which ESO calls the most advanced ground-based astronomical observatory in the world. The Mapuche people, whose language gave the telescopes their names, have their homeland some 500 kilometres to the south of Santiago de Chile. Antares ranks as the sixteenth brightest star in the night sky.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph of the observatory taken by John Colosimo with a 30-second exposure; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Over those seconds the camera gathered far more light than an eye takes in at once, and Earth's rotation turned the stars into short trails where a naked-eye observer would see points.

alt: A large telescope enclosure on a mountaintop under a star-filled Milky Way, with the red star Antares visible and stars drawn into short trails.

caption: The heart of the Milky Way over the Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: The bulging centre of the Milky Way, threaded with intricate dust clouds and the glow of billions of stars, hangs over the Chajnantor plateau in Chile's Atacama Desert. A lone stargazer stands in the middle of the foreground, taking in the view with the naked eye.

Above the dust, the planets Mars and Saturn form a clear triangle with the star Antares. On the left of the frame sits a fuzzy green smudge, almost lost in the Milky Way's glare: Comet 252P/LINEAR, which swept past Earth in April 2016. It was too faint to see without help, but long exposures like this one bring it out.

Chajnantor is among the highest and driest places on Earth. Radiation at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths is usually strongly absorbed by our atmosphere, but the height and dryness here create ideal conditions to catch it. That is why the plateau hosts ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, which examines some of the coldest objects in the Universe.
explore: The plateau is also a fine place to look up without any instruments at all. Its southern skies are exceptionally clear, a reminder of the time before artificial lighting began to crowd the sky and drown out our view of the Universe.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based long-exposure landscape photograph credited to ESO/P. Horálek; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The comet was too faint for the unaided eye, and the long exposure also records more of the Milky Way's glow than a person would see.

alt: The bright, dusty centre of the Milky Way above a high plateau, with a person standing in the foreground and a small fuzzy green comet at left.

caption: Venus, Jupiter and the Milky Way over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The buildings of ESO's La Silla Observatory sit in the foreground, while the planets Venus and Jupiter hang low in the sky and the Milky Way drifts behind them as a ribbon of stars. Venus is the largest point of light, on the left; Jupiter is the smaller dot just below it and slightly to the right.

Getting the shot took patience. Photographer Zdenek Bardon waited three nights for a sky with no clouds and low humidity. That wait was unusual here, since most nights at this site are free of clouds and rain.

La Silla owes its reputation partly to fairly low light pollution, though the lights of human settlements still show along the horizon in this view. Its elevation of 2400 metres keeps humidity exceptionally low. Moist air is a problem for astronomers and photographers alike: condensation can film over mirrors and lenses, and dense water vapour absorbs some parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
explore: The clear conditions that rewarded Bardon's wait are the same ones enjoyed by the telescopes ESO runs at La Silla, including the New Technology Telescope and the 3.6-metre telescope. The photo doubles as a showcase for the beauty of Atacama Desert skies.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Zdenek Bardon; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can collect light for longer than the eye, so the faint band of the Milky Way may look more vivid here than to someone standing at the site.

alt: Observatory buildings under a starry sky, with bright Venus and smaller Jupiter low above the horizon and the Milky Way behind them.

caption: A laser guide star beam over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A single laser beam slices upward into the night from one of the four Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory. To the left of the beam, the two Magellanic Clouds show as faint, fuzzy patches among the stars. The especially bright star to its right is Canopus, second only to Sirius in our night sky.

The laser is part of an adaptive optics system. Starlight reaching a ground-based telescope must pass through our atmosphere, and the water vapour, pollution and turbulence that make stars twinkle also blur images. The laser creates an artificial star about 90 kilometres up. By tracking how this fake star twinkles over time, astronomers can drive deformable mirrors that cancel out the distortion.
The payoff is considerable: at certain wavelengths, telescopes using adaptive optics can take images sharper than those from space telescopes.
explore: Julien Girard, an ESO staff astronomer and photo ambassador, took this picture from the platform of VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, using a compact point-and-shoot camera. A similar laser system is planned for the European Extremely Large Telescope, which will use six lasers to deliver even better images over a much larger field of view.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph taken by Julien Girard with a compact point-and-shoot camera; the packet does not publish exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Night photography builds up faint light over time, so the Magellanic Clouds may look more distinct here than they would to the eye.

alt: A thin laser beam rising from a telescope into a starry sky, with two faint fuzzy patches to its left and a bright star to its right.

caption: The Milky Way over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Observatory domes sit beneath a sky shimmering with stars at ESO's La Silla Observatory, high in Chile's Atacama Desert. A dense, bright band runs almost vertically across the frame, mottled by dark pockets of dust that block the light of stars behind them.

Every star here belongs to our own galaxy, the Milky Way, which holds billions of stars in two very different structures. A roughly spherical halo, made mostly of older stars, appears as the scattering of stars across the whole sky. A thin disc of younger stars, gas and dust forms the bright band.

Toward the top centre of the band lies a bright concentration: the central region of the galaxy. There, astronomers have measured stars moving far faster than anywhere else in the Milky Way. They take this as evidence for a supermassive black hole of some four million solar masses. It cannot be seen directly, but its enormous gravity shows in the motions of nearby stars.
explore: ESO says the domes at La Silla hold some of the world's most advanced astronomical instruments, set here beneath the very sky they are built to study. The photograph is credited to B. Tafreshi of twanight.org.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/B. Tafreshi; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way's band may appear brighter and more detailed here than to an observer on site.

alt: Observatory domes beneath a star-filled sky, with a bright, dust-mottled band of the Milky Way running almost vertically and brightest near the top centre.

caption: The Coalsack Nebula above an ALMA antenna, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: One of the antennas of ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, stands beneath the band of the Milky Way. At the very top of the frame, a pair of bright stars marks part of Crux, the Southern Cross. Just below, a dark, irregular shape is silhouetted against the galaxy's glow.

That shape is a prominent dark nebula only 600 light-years from us: a huge molecular cloud dense enough to block the light of everything behind it. Its name depends on who you ask. Most people know it as the Coalsack Nebula. In Aboriginal Australian astronomy it is the head of an emu stretched across the sky, a figure made of dust rather than stars. Inca astronomers called it Yutu, after the tinamou, a shy, partridge-like bird of South America.
Visible light cannot get through a cloud like this, but stars and galaxies hidden behind it often shine through at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths. That is exactly the range ALMA explores.
explore: ALMA is an array of 66 antennas in northern Chile. People have long been drawn to the Milky Way's flowing shape, its bright stars and planets, and the dark patches that hide parts of the sky, and different cultures have given these features their own names.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/Y. Beletsky (LCO); the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The dark nebula blocks visible light for eye and camera alike, though a camera gathering light over time may show the surrounding Milky Way more brightly than an observer would see it.

scaleExtra: The Coalsack Nebula lies just 600 light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: A radio antenna dish beneath the Milky Way, with two bright stars at the top of the frame and a dark, irregular cloud just below them.

caption: The New Technology Telescope and the Large Magellanic Cloud, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The 3.58-metre New Technology Telescope (NTT) at ESO's La Silla Observatory stands against the southern sky. Behind it, the Milky Way, our home galaxy, runs as a hazy stripe, broken by dark regions where interstellar dust blocks the light of stars beyond. To the right of the telescope floats a foggy blob: the Large Magellanic Cloud.

The Large Magellanic Cloud is a nearby irregular galaxy and a conspicuous sight in southern skies. It circles our galaxy, and evidence suggests that the interaction between the two has greatly distorted it.

Research telescopes pair large mirrors with state-of-the-art cameras to catch the faint light of distant objects. Yet beautiful astronomical pictures can also come from modest cameras. Astrophotographers often work on a wider scale than big telescopes do, and some fold the landscape into the frame, producing postcards of the Universe as seen from Earth, like this one.
explore: The photographer, Håkon Dahle, is also an accomplished professional astronomer. He shared the image through the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group, which ESO reviews regularly to pick photos for its Picture of the Week series and its gallery.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph taken by Håkon Dahle with a conventional camera; the packet does not publish exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can collect light for longer than the eye, so the Large Magellanic Cloud and the dust lanes may look more distinct here than they would in person.

alt: A telescope building under a starry sky, with the hazy, dust-streaked Milky Way behind it and a foggy patch, the Large Magellanic Cloud, to its right.

caption: The Milky Way at dawn over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Just before dawn at La Silla Observatory, an orange layer hovers over the horizon, signalling that the Sun is about to rise. Above it, the Milky Way stretches across the entire sky, dotted with dark patches where dust particles block light from behind. In the foreground stand several of the observatory's telescopes.

Closest to the camera is the Swedish–ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST), with a dish 15 metres across. It was retired in 2003, its work taken over by APEX and ALMA. On the plateau behind stand the ESO 3.6-metre telescope and, just beyond it, the Coudé Auxiliary Telescope.

SEST seems to point at a dazzling object. That is Venus, lit by the Sun and brighter than any star in the night sky. Rising from the horizon through Venus is a triangular white glow called zodiacal light: sunlight scattered by dust lying in the ecliptic, the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun.
explore: La Silla lies on the outskirts of the Chilean Atacama Desert. The two facilities that took over from SEST are the Atacama Pathfinder EXperiment telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/B. Tafreshi; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light over time, so the faint zodiacal light and the Milky Way may look more pronounced here than to someone standing at the site.

alt: Telescopes under a pre-dawn sky with an orange glow on the horizon, the Milky Way overhead, and bright Venus inside a faint triangular glow.

caption: The four lasers of the Very Large Telescope and the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Four laser beams from ESO's Very Large Telescope stab into the heart of the Milky Way. The starry scene is crossed by the vertical glow of zodiacal light, which comes from dust grains in the Solar System. It is so faint that only the darkest skies, such as those over Chile's Atacama Desert, reveal it.

Those skies have long been woven into the culture of the region's indigenous peoples, and the number four runs through their traditions. The Chakana, a recurring Andean symbol shaped like a stepped square cross, stands for four stairs or bridges leading to the upper levels of the Andean view of the cosmos.

For the Mapuche of south-central Chile, the sky is Wenu mapu, a realm of goodness and order home to deities, ancestors and kindly spirits, arranged in four layers. Names and details vary across Andean traditions, but four is consistently treated as a measure of perfection. In a sense, the VLT's four lasers, which sharpen our view of space, echo that ancient pattern.
explore: In the Mapuche vision, holy beings including four star gods (Meli wanlén) and four Moon gods (Meli Kiyén) stand against the forces of evil below. Those forces clash on Earth, a world split into four cardinal directions, each tied to different degrees of good and evil. Four signals perfection because balance needs two opposite things.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph credited to F. Millour/ESO; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Zodiacal light is faint enough to need the darkest skies, and a camera collecting light over time may show it more plainly than the eye does.

alt: Four laser beams rising from telescopes into the Milky Way, crossed by a faint vertical band of glowing light.

caption: The Milky Way over the Extremely Large Telescope under construction, Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: The band of the Milky Way flows down toward ESO's Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), whose open dome seems to catch its light, while huge cranes around the building lean in as work on the telescope moves forward. Directly above the dome sits a very bright, orange patch laced with dark filaments of gas and dust: the core of our galaxy.

Stars at the galactic centre look redder for two reasons. Many of them are old, and dust lying between us and them reddens their light, much as particles in Earth's air turn the Sun red at sunrise and sunset.

Once assembly is finished, the ELT is set to become the largest telescope in the world, and it will study the dark Atacama sky with unprecedented precision. Among its goals are probing the close surroundings of our galaxy's central supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, analysing the atmospheres of exoplanets, and exploring how galaxies form and change over time.
explore: ESO expects the telescope to tackle questions about the births and deaths of stars that astronomers cannot yet even frame, alongside many other open problems. This photograph catches it while it is still being built, beneath the very sky it will one day observe.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to C. Letelier/ESO; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the galactic core and its dark filaments may look brighter and more detailed here than they would to someone on site.

alt: The Milky Way pouring down toward a large open telescope dome ringed by construction cranes, with a bright orange patch just above the dome.

caption: The nova V392 Persei over the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Centre, imaged by Petr Horálek
story: This wide-angle view of the evening sky, looking west-northwest over the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Centre, holds a rare guest. An inset, shot with the same camera but a different lens, zooms in on the spot where a star had flared up as a nova; it is easy to pick out by its typical orange colour. ESO photo ambassador Petr Horálek captured the scene on 2 May 2018, less than a week after the centre opened.

The star is V392 Persei, a dwarf nova. Such outbursts happen in a binary system where a white dwarf pulls material from a lower-mass companion. The gas, gathered in a disc, is squeezed as it lands on the white dwarf's surface, heats up and ignites in a powerful, bright explosion.
V392 Persei went further. Only once before in the history of dwarf nova observations, with V1213 Centauri in 2009, had such a star turned into a full-fledged and far brighter nova.
explore: The timing carries a symbolic twist. The ESO Supernova building was designed to resemble a double star system much like the one behind V392 Persei, a kind of pairing that could ultimately end with one of the stars exploding as a supernova, which is where the centre gets its name.

understand.summary: This is a wide-angle ground-based photograph by Petr Horálek, with an inset taken using the same camera and a different lens; the packet does not publish exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The inset is a magnified view through a different lens, so the nova appears larger and clearer there than it would to someone simply looking up from the building.

alt: A wide view of the evening sky over a building, with a marked inset zooming in on an orange point of light, the nova V392 Persei.

caption: The Milky Way over the Danish 1.54-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way arches over the Danish 1.54-metre telescope's dome at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. In the distance, the central part of our galaxy rises beyond the ESO 3.6-metre telescope's dome, and the Magellanic Clouds appear on the right.

The Danish telescope has an important place in the hunt for planets around other stars. It was a major contributor to the PLANET project, which searched for exoplanets using microlensing. In this technique, astronomers watch for a background star to brighten briefly as a foreground star passes in front of it. The foreground star's gravity acts like a lens, and a planet orbiting it can add a small, telltale blip to the brightening.
The picture itself needed no special equipment. An ordinary digital camera gathered the light over 15 minutes of total exposure.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph taken with a normal digital camera and a total exposure of 15 minutes, credited to ESO/Z. Bardon and ProjectSoft; the colour processing is not published.
understand.eye: Fifteen minutes of exposure gathers far more light than the eye can, so the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds look much stronger here than they would in person.

alt: The Milky Way arching above a telescope dome, with the galaxy's bright centre behind a more distant dome and the Magellanic Clouds at right.

caption: The Milky Way over Valle de la Luna, Atacama Desert, Chile
story: Twisted, gnarled rock formations jut from the desert floor like old wizards' hats, while overhead the sky fills with thousands of stars and a wash of colours. This is Valle de la Luna, the "Valley of the Moon", in Chile's Atacama Desert, not far from ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, a facility in which ESO is a partner.

The name fits. Aeons of exposure to wind and weather have worn the dried-up salt beds into moon-like shapes that feel more alien than earthly. Above them, the Milky Way pours across the sky, lit by its gas and stars, with vivid red tones that come from hydrogen atoms spread throughout our galaxy.

The valley's altitude, dry air and remoteness also make it a superb spot for stargazing. Dryness matters especially for ALMA, because water vapour in the atmosphere can soak up the invisible light this radio telescope collects.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to P. Horálek/ESO; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The red hydrogen glow and many of the other colours are faint, and a camera gathering light over time may record them far more vividly than the eye.

alt: Twisted rock formations in a desert under a star-filled sky, with the Milky Way overhead tinged with red.

caption: Circumpolar star trails over an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Stars sweep in concentric circles around a single point in the sky, and the tip of one of the Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory lines up almost perfectly with that centre, so the whole sky seems to revolve around it. Chilean astrophotographer Osvaldo Castillo calls making this image one of the most incredible experiences of his career behind the camera.

The circles come from Earth spinning on its axis. Extend that axis into space and it meets the sky at a celestial pole, here the southern one, around which every star appears to wheel. Hence the name circumpolar star trails.

They are hard to make. Many long-exposure frames must be shot over several hours and combined, and the trails only appear once they come together, so a small misalignment can spoil everything. Because the telescope moves as it points to new targets, the foreground and sky also needed separate shots. Castillo took almost 300 images, trusting that his orientation to the south was right.
explore: Castillo notes that there is no way to see the result straight away while shooting. He had to rely on his calculations and alignment being accurate, and fortunately they were.

understand.summary: This is a composite of many long-exposure frames taken over several hours by Osvaldo Castillo, with separate shots for the foreground and the sky; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: An observer would see stars as points that shift slowly through the night; the trails exist only because hours of frames were combined into one picture.

alt: Stars drawn into concentric circular trails centred just above the tip of a telescope enclosure.

caption: Antu and the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The bright band of the Milky Way, packed with glowing gas, dark dust and sparkling stars, cuts through the middle of this night scene at ESO's Paranal Observatory and seems to plunge toward the glowing horizon. At the centre stands the boxy form of UT1, or Antu, one of the four Unit Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope (VLT). To the right, a smaller Auxiliary Telescope scans the sky with its dome wide open.
Together, the VLT's eight telescopes, four of them movable auxiliaries, can work as a highly sensitive interferometer, sharp enough to tell apart the two headlights of a car as far away as the Moon.

The skies here are among the clearest anywhere, as the detail in the Milky Way shows. Jupiter blazes as the large, bright object on the left. Along the horizon runs a greenish tint called airglow, faint light produced by chemiluminescence in the atmosphere. Airglow and turbulence are major reasons astronomers send telescopes such as Hubble above the atmosphere.
explore: The NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope is one example of an observatory that works high above the optical distortions that frustrate ground-based astronomers. The skies over the VLT are also some of the most photographed anywhere, prized for their clarity.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/P. Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Airglow is very faint, and a camera gathering light over time may show its greenish tint and the Milky Way's dust far more clearly than the eye.

alt: The Milky Way descending toward the horizon above a boxy telescope building, with a smaller open-domed telescope at right, a bright planet at left and a greenish glow along the horizon.

caption: The Eta Aquariids meteor shower and a line of planets near San Pedro de Atacama, Chile
story: Bright, arrow-like streaks dart across a sky crowded with sights. They are meteors from the Eta Aquariids shower, photographed by astrophotographer Petr Horálek near the Chilean town of San Pedro de Atacama, about 50 km from the Chajnantor site that hosts APEX and ALMA, facilities co-owned by ESO. The meteors are debris left behind by Halley's comet.

Low in the sky shines Venus. Stacked above it in a neat line are Jupiter, then red Mars, then Saturn, a planetary conjunction of a kind that can come decades apart. The planets follow the zodiacal light, a faint pillar of glow reaching up toward the bright, star-packed centre of the Milky Way.

Zodiacal light is sunlight reflected by dust in the plane of the Solar System. That dust comes from asteroids, passing comets and even inner planets such as Mars. It is often seen from dark sites like ESO's observatories soon after sunset or before sunrise, as it is here above a red sunset over the mountains and volcanoes around Chajnantor.
explore: ESO describes the frame as packed with astronomical phenomena: a meteor shower, a planetary line-up, zodiacal light and the Milky Way, all above a sunset glow. The shower reached its peak in early May of the year the picture was published.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Petr Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Meteors flash by in moments and zodiacal light is faint, so a camera gathering light over time can show more of both at once than an observer would notice.

alt: Meteor streaks across a starry sky, with a line of bright planets rising along a faint pillar of light toward the Milky Way, above red-lit mountains.

caption: Star trails over the BlackGEM telescopes, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Stars swirl in circles above ESO's La Silla Observatory in this long exposure, all turning around the south celestial pole as Earth rotates. Hidden in the vortex are a few familiar objects, now barely recognisable: the Carina Nebula as a bright magenta smudge left of centre, and the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds as blue smudges near the top centre and to the right of centre.

Beneath the trails, two of the three BlackGEM telescopes gaze upward. They are built and run by KU Leuven, Radboud University and the Netherlands Research School for Astronomy (NOVA). The third, on the right, was still being built when the photo was taken, with a platform but no dome yet.

BlackGEM is designed to chase dramatic cosmic collisions, such as merging black holes and neutron stars. When detectors like LIGO and Virgo pick up gravitational waves from such an event, BlackGEM will sweep wide areas of sky for its visible light, and telescopes including ESO's VLT can then follow up.
explore: The project aims eventually to grow to 15 telescopes able to carry out extensive surveys of the night sky. Its role is to help astronomers better understand some of the most elusive phenomena in the Universe.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure star-trail photograph by Zdeněk Bardon; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points, not arcs; the circular trails build up only because the camera recorded Earth's rotation over a long exposure.

alt: Circular star trails over two small domed telescopes and an empty platform, with a magenta smudge left of centre and blue smudges near the top and right.

caption: The Milky Way seen through a crystal ball, Atacama Desert, Chile
story: The glimmering arch of the Milky Way, full of stars and tangled patches of gas and dust, is seen here through a crystal ball, giving an unusual take on our home galaxy. ESO Photo Ambassador Juan Carlos Muñoz-Mateos made the picture, hoping to share what it feels like to look up from the Atacama Desert, one of the darkest and most barren places on Earth and home to ESO's Paranal Observatory.

The night sky has fascinated people for as long as there have been people to look. Thousands of years ago, ancient cultures tracked celestial objects to mark seasons and time, to tell stories and to make sense of the world.

Photographers turned their lenses skyward almost as soon as photography existed, yet the first star was not captured on camera until 1850. Camera technology grew more complex in the decades that followed, and pictures made with light from across the electromagnetic spectrum are now the backbone of modern astronomy.
explore: Modern stargazers feel much the same pull toward the night sky as those ancient observers did, and photographers have always been chasing the same prize: a dark sky scattered with countless points of light.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph by Juan Carlos Muñoz-Mateos, taken through a crystal ball; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way's gas and dust may appear more distinct here than to an unaided observer.

alt: The arch of the Milky Way, with its stars and dark patches of dust, seen through a crystal ball.

caption: The ALMA entrance sign under the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: It might look like a sign pointing the way into the Milky Way, but it actually marks the entrance to the ALMA Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert, with the glowing band of our galaxy also in the frame. The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, run by ESO with international partners, studies light from the coldest corners of the Universe.

ALMA works at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which water vapour in Earth's atmosphere readily absorbs. That is why it sits on the Chajnantor Plateau in the Andes, among the highest and driest spots on the planet, at an altitude of 5000 metres.

Unlike our eyes, or the camera that took this photo, ALMA uses interferometry to reveal fine detail. It combines the light gathered by 66 high-precision antennas so that the array behaves like a single telescope as wide as the greatest distance between its antennas. That has produced some of the most detailed images of the Milky Way, including filaments of dense gas and dust at its core.
explore: We cannot travel to the glowing band of our galaxy, but ESO suggests that images like ALMA's are among the closest things we have to a gateway for admiring the Milky Way and everything it contains.

understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way may look brighter here than to someone standing by the sign.

caption: The Magellanic Clouds over two Auxiliary Telescopes, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Two Auxiliary Telescopes point skyward in the Chilean desert while the Magellanic Clouds, the Milky Way's two biggest satellite galaxies, shine above them. A human silhouette stands on the right, and the background holds the colourful, extremely faint airglow of our atmosphere.

French photographer Julien Looten set out to show two kinds of pairs, one cosmic and one technological. The Magellanic Clouds are dwarf galaxies that travel through space alongside our own, and many indigenous cultures in the southern hemisphere named them after water wells. The Auxiliary Telescopes, in turn, are companions to the VLT's larger Unit Telescopes, feeding light into ESO's Very Large Telescope Interferometer.

Looten describes the scene as showing the "immensity of the cosmos". Against that backdrop, the small human figure is a reminder of how tiny we are beside cosmic objects and even beside our telescopes. We can study the vastness of the Universe, but our time on Earth is brief, and sometimes the best response is simply to watch and admire.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Julien Looten; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The airglow is extremely faint, and a camera gathering light over time may reveal its colours far more readily than the eye.

caption: Star trails over the mountains near La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Streaks of starlight seem to rain down onto the surrounding mountains in this star-trail image from ESO's La Silla Observatory. A wisp of snow lies on the distant peaks, soft clouds hang below the observatory near the horizon on the left, and a slightly darker, redder area on the right is an open copper mine.

Real rain is rare here. The Atacama is one of the driest places on Earth, and significant rain or snow falls at La Silla only once every few years, usually during an unusually warm event such as El Niño. Those dry skies make it an excellent place to observe.

Diana Juncher, an astronomy PhD student at Denmark's Niels Bohr Institute, took the picture on 21 May 2013, standing only around 20 metres from the Danish 1.54-metre telescope. She was spending two weeks at La Silla observing exoplanets toward the centre of our galaxy. Star trails like these come from long exposures that record the stars' apparent motion as Earth turns.
explore: The reddish open mine at the right of the frame hints at the local economy: copper is Chile's biggest economic asset, and Chile out-produces every other country in copper by a wide margin.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure star-trail photograph by Diana Juncher; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: To the eye the stars would be steady points; the streaks appear only because the long exposure recorded their apparent motion as Earth rotated.

alt: Star trails streaking down toward snow-dusted mountains, with low clouds at left and a reddish open mine at right.

caption: The arc of the Milky Way over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The bright arc of the Milky Way spans the sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory. On the ground stand two instruments: to the right, the dome of ESO's 3.6-metre optical telescope; to the left, the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope's silvery dish. That dish was retired in 2003 to make way for APEX and ALMA, yet it still seems to gaze hopefully upward.

Hanging from the top of the arc is a striking red feature, the Gum Nebula. Like similar regions along the Milky Way, it is an emission nebula: gas made to glow by radiation from nearby bright stars. Dark filaments of dust break up the band, and inside them new stars are forming that will join the display in the millennia ahead.

Beneath the arc lies the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that accompanies our own. Its sibling, the Small Magellanic Cloud, sits below it, just right of the dish. Over on the right, Jupiter shines against the faint gegenschein, a glow that only the darkest skies reveal.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek took the image. La Silla ranks among the world's best astronomical sites, known for dark skies and clear air, and a display that most people rarely get to see is an everyday sight at observing sites of its kind.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Petr Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Faint features such as the gegenschein and the red glow of the Gum Nebula may show up far more strongly in a camera that gathers light over time than to the eye.

alt: The Milky Way arching over a telescope dome at right and a dish antenna at left, with a red nebula at the top of the arc, two fuzzy patches below and a bright planet at right.

caption: Star trails over Yepun, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Bright star trails circle the south celestial pole above one of the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), which is lit by moonlight. The pole, the point the trails wheel around, sits within Octans, the Octant, a constellation of the southern sky.

Each arc traces the path a star appears to follow across the sky as Earth slowly turns. Rather than a single frame, many exposures were taken over time and then combined to produce the circular tracks.

The telescope is Yepun, one of the four Unit Telescopes that make up the VLT at Paranal. After the site's inauguration in 1999, the telescopes received names from the language of the native Mapuche people. Antu, Kueyen, Melipal and Yepun stand for the Sun, the Moon, the Southern Cross and Venus, four striking sights in the sky.
explore: The photographer, ESO Photo Ambassador Farid Char, works at ESO's La Silla–Paranal Observatory and belongs to the team testing the site of the future European Extremely Large Telescope. At the time, ESO expected that telescope to become the world's largest optical/near-infrared telescope once completed in the early 2020s.

understand.summary: This is a composite of many exposures taken over time by Farid Char and combined to show star trails; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: An observer sees stars as points; the circular tracks appear only because many exposures recorded Earth's rotation.

alt: Circular star trails around a point in the sky above a moonlit telescope enclosure.

caption: The Milky Way rising over the control building, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A rising Milky Way arcs over the control building at Paranal Observatory, which sits beneath it like the treasure waiting at the end of a rainbow in the sky. ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky took the picture.

The building is the nerve centre of the observatory. From here, staff run and maintain the Very Large Telescope (VLT), the VLT Interferometer, the VLT Survey Telescope (VST) and VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy. Astronomers, telescope and instrument operators, and engineers are on site 24 hours a day to keep everything working at its best.

It sits a little below the summit's main observing platform, on a shelf of the mountain. The four Unit Telescopes, the four Auxiliary Telescopes and the two survey telescopes each have their own area in the central control room, linked to a huge array of computers. Running a night is more than aiming a telescope: operators monitor its status continuously and tune the instruments before exposures.
explore: The team must also move and store the large volumes of data the telescopes produce and check the quality of results as they arrive. Not even the view outside the window distracts them from keeping Paranal among the world's most productive and powerful ground-based observatories.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Yuri Beletsky; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way may look brighter and more detailed here than from the building's doorstep.

alt: The Milky Way rising in an arc above the observatory's control building.

caption: The Milky Way over a tower at Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way streaks across the sky above Chile's Atacama Desert. Dark wisps of interstellar dust mingle with the shine of hot gas and billions of stars, so the band looks like the thick smoke trail left by a rocket after launch. Below this turbulent sight, a tower at ESO's Paranal Observatory stands calmly under the evening sky.

The observatory hosts ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), which combines four Unit Telescopes with four Auxiliary Telescopes that can be moved around. Various combinations of them can act as an interferometer, pooling the light they collect so astronomers can study the Universe in very fine detail.

The VLT has notched up many scientific firsts. Among them is following individual stars that race around our galaxy's centre at speeds never measured before. Motion that fast signals a powerful gravitational field, and it points to a supermassive black hole hiding there, known as Sagittarius A*.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/Y. Beletsky; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the dust and glowing gas of the Milky Way may look more dramatic here than to someone standing at the tower.

alt: A dusty, glowing band of the Milky Way streaking across the sky above a tower at an observatory.

caption: The centre of the Milky Way between the NTT and the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The centre of the Milky Way rises between two telescopes at ESO's La Silla Observatory, its light splattered among dark clouds. Between the buildings glow two nebulae in the constellation Sagittarius: the Trifid Nebula on the left and the Lagoon Nebula on the right.

Both look red because young stars inside them ionise hydrogen atoms, making the gas glow. The Trifid also carries a blue tint, from dust reflecting some of that starlight. Most of the dust here, though, shows up as dark clouds. Without nearby stars to light it, interstellar dust blocks whatever lies behind and appears black against the stars.

On the left stands the New Technology Telescope (NTT), a pioneer of active optics, which keeps a telescope mirror in shape during observations despite distortions caused by its weight or by temperature. On the right is the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, home to the exoplanet-hunting instruments HARPS and NIRPS.
explore: That second telescope means a great deal to the photographer, José Rodrigues. He grew up with a poster of it on his bedroom wall, dreaming of one day using it to find exoplanets, and he has since realised that dream as an exoplanet researcher.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by José Rodrigues; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The red and blue tints of these nebulae are faint, and a camera gathering light over time may show them far more clearly than the eye.

alt: The bright centre of the Milky Way between two telescope buildings, with two small red nebulae between them and dark dust clouds across the band.

caption: The Carina Nebula above an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A big pink spot glows in the dark sky directly over an Auxiliary Telescope, one of four belonging to ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal Observatory. That spot is the Carina Nebula, a massive star-forming region. The southern sky here also holds the Magellanic Clouds.

For French photographer Julien Looten, the view was special. The Carina Nebula cannot be seen from the northern hemisphere, and he called finally seeing it with his own eyes an unforgettable moment. Paranal's southern location and exceptionally dark skies made the picture possible.

The nebula hosts Eta Carinae, two massive stars with short lives that are throwing off great quantities of material. Astronomers have studied the structure of this cloud in detail with the VLT Interferometer, linking three Auxiliary Telescopes like the one pictured into a huge virtual telescope. The upheaval at Eta Carinae makes a sharp contrast with the stillness of the Atacama Desert below.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Julien Looten; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Looten could see the Carina Nebula with his own eyes, though a camera gathering light over time likely records its pink colour more strongly than the eye perceives it.

caption: A self-portrait under the centre of the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: A still, dark figure stands on Earth beneath a brilliant night sky filled by the vast spray of stars and dust that marks the centre of the Milky Way. The figure is astronomer Alan Fitzsimmons, who took this self-portrait between observing sessions at ESO's La Silla Observatory.

Even seasoned astronomers find it hard to resist pausing a busy observing schedule to stare up at the rich southern sky. ESO's observatories stand in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile, a sparsely populated region where very dark nights meet extremely clear air, both vital for high-quality observations.

La Silla is ESO's first observatory, inaugurated in 1969, and it hosts several telescopes with mirrors up to 3.6 metres across. With more than 300 clear nights a year, it is ideal for advanced instruments, and just as good for simply standing still and gazing up.
explore: The picture plays on contrast: a simple, motionless silhouette set against a sky full of light. Fitzsimmons submitted it to the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group, which ESO checks regularly to choose images for its Picture of the Week series and its picture gallery.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based self-portrait photograph by Alan Fitzsimmons; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way's centre may look brighter and richer here than it did to Fitzsimmons himself.

caption: The Andromeda Galaxy and Messier 33 above Yepun, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Bright stars and distant galaxies speckle the clear Chilean sky above Yepun, the fourth of the four Unit Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope (VLT), whose name means Venus. On the left, a fairly prominent galaxy forms a streak across the sky: Messier 31, better known as the Andromeda Galaxy.
Up and to the right of that smudge is a bright star, Beta Andromedae, also called Mirach. Continue roughly along the same line and you reach a second galaxy at the top of the frame, Messier 33.

Astronomers think the pair once interacted, leaving a bridge of hydrogen gas stretched across the gap between them. The picture's title calls them two naked-eye galaxies: systems far beyond our own Milky Way that can still be spotted without a telescope.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by ESO photo ambassador Babak Tafreshi; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The two galaxies are faint smudges to the eye, and a camera gathering light over time shows them more clearly than an observer would see them.

alt: Stars and two faint galaxies, one a streak at left and one at the top, above a large telescope enclosure, with a bright star between them.

caption: Astrophotographers beneath the Milky Way at Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: At the lower left of this southern sky, two figures stand beside one of the Auxiliary Telescopes that serve the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) at ESO's Paranal Observatory. They are astrophotographers Yuri Beletsky and Babak Tafreshi, both ESO Photo Ambassadors, photographed by a third, Petr Horálek.

Above them, the bright band of the Milky Way dominates the sky, with the red Gum Nebula (Gum 12) at the top of the frame. Toward the centre right, the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of our galaxy's satellites, makes an especially bright blotch just below Canopus. Canopus is the brightest star both in this view and in the southern constellation of Carina.

Along the bottom of the image, a green and reddish shimmer seems to rise from the horizon. This is airglow, faint light given off by Earth's own atmosphere. It is the reason the night sky is never completely dark.

understand.eye: Airglow and the Gum Nebula are faint, and a camera gathering light over time may reveal their colours far more readily than the eye.

caption: The Milky Way and laser guide stars over the Auxiliary Telescope stairs, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A staircase at ESO's Paranal Observatory leads up toward a sky thick with stars. The galactic centre can, at first glance, pass for a dragon with a strange orange tongue. Bright yellow beams cross the scene: laser guide stars fired from the Very Large Telescope (VLT), which stands to the right, just outside the frame.

The lasers create artificial stars high in the atmosphere. The telescope's adaptive optics system uses them to correct for atmospheric blurring and make the sharpest possible observations from the ground. For the VLT, this is simply an ordinary night's work.

The stairs give outside access to the VLT's smaller Auxiliary Telescopes, and they make a fine spot for photography. Standing at the top, at 2635 metres above sea level plus some twenty steps, you can see a wealth of stars that stay hidden elsewhere, because Paranal has the darkest skies of any major observatory on Earth.
explore: Short of travelling to space, ESO suggests, few places make you feel closer to the stars than the top of this staircase in Chile's Atacama Desert, where the sky feels just one small step beyond the last stair.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to F. Millour/ESO; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way's colours and dust may look more vivid here than to someone on the stairs.

alt: A staircase leading up toward a star-filled sky, with the centre of the Milky Way above and bright yellow laser beams crossing it.

caption: A lunar eclipse sequence over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A trail of Moon images arcs over ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal, recording a lunar eclipse in a photographic sequence three hours long. In the middle of the trail, the Moon darkens and turns red as it passes into Earth's shadow. Behind it, the stars also trace long trails.

The red colour comes from sunlight that is scattered by Earth's atmosphere before it reaches the Moon. Both the Moon's path and the star trails are produced by Earth's rotation, a familiar feature of long-exposure night-sky photographs. The eclipse took place on 20-21 January 2019 and could be seen from the Americas.

Paranal's high altitude and lack of light pollution from towns keep its stars crisp. Moonlight, though, remains a nuisance for observations made in visible light, so astronomers must take the Moon's position and phase into account when planning and carrying out their work.
explore: Astronomers also watched this eclipse with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope, hoping to learn more about possible signs of life on worlds orbiting other stars. ESO's blog has more on that study.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photographic sequence spanning three hours, credited to ESO/J. C. Muñoz-Mateos; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: An observer would see a single Moon slowly darkening and reddening; the sequence places its positions side by side and turns the stars into trails.

alt: A curved trail of Moon images, reddened in the middle, arcing over large telescope enclosures, with star trails in the background.

caption: Sunset behind the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The Sun is going down behind ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile's Atacama Desert, with three of its four Unit Telescopes in view. Only a dozen minutes after sunset, stars are already scattered across the cloudless sky. The bright star Sirius is visible, and the famous constellation of Orion, the hunter, hangs over the nearest unit telescope's dome.
Prime observing conditions here come down to location. ESO's Paranal Observatory sits at an altitude of 2600 m in one of the world's driest regions, where skies are exceptionally clear.

The photograph, credited to ESO/P. Horálek, catches the brief interval between day and night. As darkness deepens, the sky will reveal more and more detail, until conditions are right for the telescopes to begin a night of world-leading science observations.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/P. Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: In the twilight glow the eye picks out only the brightest stars at first; a camera may already record more of them than an observer would notice.

alt: Telescope enclosures silhouetted against a sunset, with stars appearing in a clear sky and the constellation Orion above the nearest dome.

caption: The New Technology Telescope and the ESO 3.6-metre telescope under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: With the Milky Way as a backdrop, two telescopes crown a hill at the centre of this view of ESO's La Silla Observatory. The rectangular building on the left houses the New Technology Telescope (NTT), and the dome on the right belongs to the ESO 3.6-metre telescope. Set up in the 1960s, La Silla was the first observatory ESO built in Chile.

The 3.58-metre NTT opened in 1989 as the world's first telescope with a computer-controlled main mirror. That mirror is flexible, and during observations its shape is continually adjusted to keep images as sharp as possible. The technique, called active optics, is now used on all major modern telescopes, among them the future European Extremely Large Telescope and the Very Large Telescope on Cerro Paranal.
Other telescopes share the site, including the Swedish–ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST) and TAROT, a robotic instrument that watches for fast-changing events such as gamma-ray bursts.
explore: The photographer, ESO Photo Ambassador José Joaquín Pérez, works as an agricultural engineer when he is not photographing the night sky, devoting his time to protecting crops in central Chile.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by José Joaquín Pérez; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way may appear brighter and more detailed here than to someone standing on the site.

alt: A rectangular telescope building and a domed telescope on a hill, with the Milky Way behind them.

caption: The Milky Way arching over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way arches over ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT). Three of its four Unit Telescopes sit centred beneath the arch, while the fourth is hidden at the right edge of the frame. Further back on the right stands a smaller instrument, the VLT Survey Telescope (VST).

The sky looks divided: a greenish haze fills the left side and a reddish one the right. Both are airglow, light produced by chemical processes high in Earth's atmosphere, and its colour depends on which atoms or molecules are excited. Airglow is extremely faint and shows up only in the darkest places on Earth, such as the Atacama Desert, since artificial light, even from far away, easily overwhelms it.

For French astrophotographer Julien Looten, the picture carries symbolic weight: it marked the end of the night. Keeping skies this pristine matters for cutting-edge research, and it also lets more people experience the magic of a truly dark night, as Looten did here.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Julien Looten; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Airglow is extremely faint, and a camera gathering light over time can reveal its green and red tints far more readily than the eye.

alt: The Milky Way arching over three large telescope enclosures and a smaller telescope, with a greenish glow on the left of the sky and a reddish glow on the right.

caption: Satellite reflections over the southern Cherenkov Telescope Array site, Atacama Desert, Chile
story: Hundreds of astronomical objects fill this sky, among them star clusters, nebulae, dust clouds and whole galaxies; the most prominent are the Magellanic Clouds, Large and Small, at upper right. At the far right, though, something much closer grabs attention: a silver arc streaking across the sky. It is really two closely spaced lines, made by sunlight glinting off the antennae of two Iridium communication satellites orbiting Earth.

The dry, barren ground below may look empty, but it has been picked to host the southern component of the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), a planned set of 99 antennas that will search this sky for high-energy gamma rays. This kind of electromagnetic radiation is given off by the Universe's hottest, most powerful objects: supermassive black holes, supernovae and perhaps even leftovers of the Big Bang.

Gamma rays never reach the ground, because Earth's atmosphere stops them. Instead, the CTA will look for Cherenkov radiation, faint blue flashes produced when gamma rays strike particles in the air, and trace each one back to its cosmic origin.
explore: Like its neighbour, ESO's Very Large Telescope, the CTA needs a dry, isolated location to work well, and the Atacama Desert fits that need perfectly. The photograph is credited to P. Horálek/ESO/CTAO.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by P. Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the many faint clusters, nebulae and galaxies here may be far more obvious than to an observer on the ground.

alt: A starry sky over a barren desert, with two fuzzy patches at upper right and a thin silver arc streaking across the far right.

caption: Laser guide stars and the Carina Nebula over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Huge orange beams of light shoot into the sky, looking at first like some fearsome cosmic weapon. The reality is far more peaceful: a mix of gas, dust and powerful lasers above ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile, home of the Very Large Telescope (VLT). The Carina Nebula shows as a pink cloud in the clear sky.

The Carina Nebula is one of the largest nebulae in the southern night sky and an ideal target for the VLT. It is an enormous cloud of dust and gas, and stars inside it ionise the gas and make it glow.

The lasers belong to the Adaptive Optics Facility on one of the VLT's 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes, seen here in full operation. The beams excite sodium particles high in the atmosphere, which then glow, forming artificial stars. By watching these, the telescope can measure how Earth's atmosphere blurs its view and correct for it.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/G. Hüdepohl; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera gathering light over time may show the nebula's pink glow and the laser beams more strongly than the eye would see them.

alt: Orange laser beams rising from telescopes into a clear starry sky that holds a pink cloud, the Carina Nebula.

caption: The Milky Way and a full Moon over ALMA antennas, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Several antennas belonging to ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, a cutting-edge observatory, stand high in the Chilean Andes. Over the red-tinted horizon, a full Moon glows brightly, and above the antennas glides a bright streak like a cosmic caterpillar: the Milky Way.

The galaxy's bulge of gas and its intricate dust lanes stand out clearly against the star-filled sky. Pink patches show where young stars have heated and ionised the surrounding gas. The brightest part of the band is the very heart of our galaxy, which lies roughly 25 000 light-years from Earth.

ALMA's home, the Chajnantor Plateau, lies some 5000 metres above sea level. At that altitude, crystal-clear views of the sky come almost every night, as this picture shows. The photograph is credited to Y. Beletsky (LCO)/ESO.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera gathering light over time may show the pink gas patches and dust lanes more distinctly than the eye would, especially with a bright full Moon in the sky.

scaleExtra: The heart of the Milky Way lies approximately 25 000 light-years from Earth, according to ESO.
alt: Antenna dishes under a starry sky, with a full Moon over a red-tinted horizon and the bright, dusty band of the Milky Way above.

caption: A photographer on the Very Large Telescope platform by moonlight, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Seated on a railing on the observing platform of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), a lone figure looks out under the night sky. It is ESO Photo Ambassador Gianluca Lombardi, who took this self-portrait with a remote shutter release and a 30-second exposure.

The Moon is up, blazing as a bright light because of the long exposure, and it is about to slip behind Unit Telescope 4, Yepun. Moonlit shadows stretch across the platform, which is 200 metres wide. The other three Unit Telescopes stand behind: from left to right, Antu, Kueyen and Melipal, names from the indigenous Mapuche language. On the left, in front of Antu, is one of the four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes, recognisable by its round enclosure.

The VLT stands on Cerro Paranal, 2600 metres up in the Atacama Desert of Chile, among the driest places on the planet. Conditions are so good that on a clear night without the Moon, the Milky Way alone can cast shadows.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based self-portrait by Gianluca Lombardi, taken with a remote shutter release and a 30-second exposure; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The long exposure makes the Moon look like a blazing light and brightens the moonlit scene well beyond what the eye would see in a moment.
