caption: A panorama of the Very Large Telescope under a moonlit sky, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: This panoramic photograph, spanning approximately 230 degrees, takes in ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) and a broad slice of sky. The four large Unit Telescopes dominate the foreground, and nearby sit the four round enclosures of the 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes, one on the left and three on the right. On the left, what looks like a rippling ocean is actually the cloud layer below the mountaintop.

Cerro Paranal is so high, at 2600 metres, that those clouds lie beneath it; the Pacific Ocean really is in that direction, hidden under them. Above the clouds glows the Moon, lighting both the telescopes and the sky, and just above it a bright point that looks like a star is the planet Jupiter.

Other familiar sights are scattered across the sky. The tight group of stars near the top middle is the Pleiades, or Seven Sisters. Capella shines above the second Unit Telescope from the left, while Pollux and Castor, the heads of Gemini, appear above and slightly right of the rightmost one.
explore: Above the shadowed Auxiliary Telescope on the right sits the open cluster Praesepe, also called the Beehive Cluster, with the bright star Procyon above it near the top of the frame. The Unit Telescopes' mirrors, 8.2 metres across, let astronomers see things four billion times fainter than the eye can. ESO Photo Ambassador Gerhard Hüdepohl took the panorama.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based panoramic photograph by Gerhard Hüdepohl covering about 230 degrees; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: No eye takes in a 230-degree sweep at once, and the camera also records the moonlit scene with more light than an observer would perceive.

alt: A wide panorama of four large telescope enclosures and smaller round domes on a mountaintop, with a sea of clouds and a bright Moon at left under a starry sky.

caption: Star trails and a laser beam over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Long arcs of starlight curve around the south celestial pole above Paranal Observatory. An illuminated road below winds up the mountain toward the observatory, where two of the four Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) and the VST stand on the summit of Cerro Paranal. An orange beacon sweeps through the sky: the laser beams from one of those Unit Telescopes.

Pictures like this make our planet's motion visible. Earth travels around the Sun on an elliptical path, but it also spins on its axis, and that rotation makes the stars appear to shift position and wheel across the sky in long arcs.

To capture this motion, photographer Fred Kamphues took several long-exposure shots and stacked them together. The long exposure also accentuates the laser, stretching it into the broad orange sweep seen here.

understand.summary: This is a stack of several long-exposure photographs by Fred Kamphues; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points and a laser as a thin beam; the stacked long exposures turn the stars into arcs and smear the laser into a sweeping band.

alt: Star trails arcing around a point in the sky above a mountaintop observatory, with a lit road winding up the slope and an orange laser beam sweeping across the sky.

caption: A laser aimed at the Galactic Centre from Yepun, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A laser beam shoots out of Yepun, Unit Telescope 4 of ESO's Very Large Telescope, pointing straight at the centre of our galaxy. Behind the 8.2-metre telescope spreads the Milky Way, a sweep of countless stars and dust. The view is very wide, spanning about 180 degrees, and on the right stands one of the 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes, which are used for interferometry.
The beam creates an artificial star. Working with the adaptive optics system, it lets the telescope record images and spectra free of the blurring that Earth's atmosphere normally adds.

ESO astronomer Yuri Beletsky took the picture on 10 May 2010. At that moment, the SINFONI instrument and the laser guide star facility were in use by astronomers Stefan Gillessen and Hauke Enkel, who were studying the Milky Way's centre, home to a lurking supermassive black hole.

understand.summary: This is a very wide-angle ground-based photograph by Yuri Beletsky, covering about 180 degrees; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The camera takes in a far wider sweep of sky at once than the eye, and it may record the Milky Way's dust and stars more vividly too.

alt: A laser beam rising from a large telescope enclosure toward the bright centre of the Milky Way, with a smaller telescope on the right, in a very wide view.

caption: Zodiacal light, airglow and the Milky Way, Chile
story: Three bands of light share this sky, and a lone figure stands at the centre watching them: ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi, during ESO's UHD Expedition. The first band is the faint glow reaching up from the horizon just below the middle of the frame. This is zodiacal light, sunlight scattered by cosmic dust lying in the plane of Earth's orbit.

The second, red band hugs the horizon at lower left. It is airglow, light from Earth's own upper atmosphere, driven by several processes: cosmic rays, photoionised atoms recombining, and chemical reactions involving oxygen, nitrogen, hydroxyl, sodium and lithium.

The third band, high overhead, is the Milky Way, our home galaxy, made of billions of stars of every kind. Thick layers of interstellar dust hide many of them from the human eye and give the band its familiar mottled look.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/B. Tafreshi; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Zodiacal light and airglow are faint, and a camera gathering light over time may show them, especially the airglow's red colour, more clearly than the eye.

alt: A person standing beneath the night sky, with a faint glow rising from the horizon, a red glow at lower left and the Milky Way high above.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Stars wheel around the southern celestial pole through a night at ESO's La Silla Observatory in northern Chile. The fuzzy sections in the trails on the right come from the Magellanic Clouds, two small galaxies that neighbour the Milky Way.

The dome in the picture houses ESO's 3.6-metre telescope and HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, which ESO calls the world's foremost exoplanet hunter. In the lower right, a rectangular building holds the 0.25-metre TAROT telescope, designed to respond fast whenever a gamma-ray burst is spotted.

La Silla was ESO's first observing site and is still among the leading observatories of the southern hemisphere. Beyond the 3.6-metre, it hosts the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope and the New Technology Telescope, whose mirror is 3.58 metres across. The NTT was the first telescope to use active optics, making it the forerunner of every large modern telescope.

understand.summary: This is a star-trail photograph by Iztok Bončina, recording the stars' motion over the night; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points; the trails build up only because the camera recorded Earth's rotation over time.

alt: Circular star trails over a telescope dome, with fuzzy patches in the trails on the right and a rectangular building at lower right.

caption: The arch of the Milky Way over the control building, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Seen from the control building of ESO's Paranal Observatory, home of the Very Large Telescope (VLT), the Milky Way forms a great arch over the Chilean night, with the Magellanic Clouds to its left. The bright area toward the top left of the arc is the galactic centre, 27 000 light-years away.

Our galaxy measures between 100 000 and 200 000 light-years across and holds billions of stars besides the Sun. The Sun takes almost 250 million years to circle the galactic centre once, and it has completed approximately 20 such orbits since it formed.

Those two fuzzy patches, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, are among our galaxy's neighbours, orbiting at about 160 000 and 200 000 light-years respectively. Both dwarf galaxies are irregular in shape, possibly because of gravitational tugs between the two and from the Milky Way itself.
explore: Paranal's telescopes can be thought of as its eyes, and the control building as its brain. Besides offices, it houses the control room, where every telescope and instrument is operated and aimed at its targets, and where a first check of the incoming data takes place.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/M. Zamani; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds may look brighter here than they would to someone outside the building.

scaleExtra: ESO gives the Milky Way's diameter as between 100 000 and 200 000 light-years, with the galactic centre 27 000 light-years away.
alt: The Milky Way arching across a night sky over an observatory building, with two fuzzy patches, the Magellanic Clouds, on the left.

caption: The Milky Way over an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The glistening band of the Milky Way spans the sky over ESO's Paranal Observatory, the organisation's flagship site in the Atacama Desert. Below it, one of the Very Large Telescope's Auxiliary Telescopes still has its round dome shut, as if asleep and missing the show. Broad lanes of dark cloud cut through the band's bright core.

Those dark nebulae block the light of stars lying behind them, so those regions only seem to hold fewer stars. From the Sun's position in a spiral arm, some 25 000 light-years out from the centre, we get an excellent view of the galactic core, as Chilean astrophotographer Alexis Trigo shows here.

People long ago were unsure what this milky streak was and named it for its looks. Galileo Galilei changed that when he aimed a small telescope he had built at it and found it was made of countless stars. Today astronomers reckon it holds some 100 to 400 billion stars of every age, mass and colour.
explore: Gazing at this shining band has been a remarkable experience for people throughout history. Much about our home galaxy is still unknown, and ESO looks forward to whatever revolutionary findings its upcoming Extremely Large Telescope may bring.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Alexis Trigo; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the galactic core and its dark lanes may look brighter and sharper here than to someone on site.

scaleExtra: The Sun lies about 25 000 light-years from the centre of the Milky Way, according to ESO.
alt: The bright band of the Milky Way crossed by dark dust lanes, above a small telescope with a closed spherical dome.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Bright star trails fill the sky over ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, curving into near-perfect concentric arcs and circles. At the centre of the frame stands the retired Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, while the ESO 3.6-metre telescope crowns the mountain on the left, glowing with activity.

The trails come from Earth turning on its axis. As the planet rotates, the stars seem to drift across the sky, slowly drawing those rings. Recording them takes a long exposure, so a photograph like this is really a record of time passing.

HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, is installed on the 3.6-metre telescope. It hunts for exoplanets by measuring the tiny wobble of a star as an unseen planet circles it, tugging the star back and forth over each orbit.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure star-trail photograph credited to ESO/B. Tafreshi; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points; the rings appear only because the long exposure recorded the sky turning.

alt: Concentric circular star trails over a dish telescope at centre and a lit telescope dome on a mountain at left.

caption: Zodiacal light and the Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Toward the centre left of this picture, the Milky Way, rich in nebulae, stars and gas clouds, rises above the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal Observatory. On the right, a lovely, almost triangular band of diffuse light arcs above the horizon, competing for attention.

That band is zodiacal light. It lies along the ecliptic, the path the Sun appears to trace across our sky. The glow comes from sunlight scattered by dust in the space between the planets, spread through the plane of the Solar System.

Because it follows the ecliptic, the glow falls within the Zodiac, the band of sky that reaches eight degrees on either side of the ecliptic and holds the traditional zodiacal constellations. That is where the phenomenon gets its name.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to Y. Beletsky (LCO)/ESO; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Zodiacal light is diffuse and faint, and a camera gathering light over time may show it more plainly than the eye would.

alt: The Milky Way rising at centre left above large telescope enclosures, with a faint triangular band of light arcing above the horizon at right.

caption: Star trails over the Auxiliary Telescopes, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Long, bright stripes streak across the dark sky over three of the four Auxiliary Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) at ESO's Paranal Observatory. Each stripe is a star trail, the apparent track of a single star as Earth rotates.

Trails like these also bring out the stars' natural colours, and colour is a guide to temperature. According to ESO, the reddest stars are about 1000 degrees Celsius, while the hottest, which look blue, reach a few tens of thousands of degrees Celsius. Those colours are on show here in the trails above the domes.

The photographer, ESO Photo Ambassador Babak A. Tafreshi, worked under an extremely clear sky free of light pollution, thanks to the remote, high location in Chile. Those conditions are what make such a vivid display of light possible.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure star-trail photograph by Babak A. Tafreshi; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points; the trails come from Earth's rotation during the exposure, and ESO notes the technique also enhances the stars' natural colours.

alt: Long bright star trails in shades from red to blue over three small telescope domes.

caption: A stream of star trails over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Smeared trails of starlight pour across the sky above ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) and its Auxiliary Telescopes at Paranal Observatory. Below the stream, the telescopes' own motion shows up as blurred flickers, while the stars' apparent drift across the sky, caused by Earth's rotation, leaves long streaks.

To get this result, ESO Photo Ambassador Gianluca Lombardi combined many long-exposure images. Stacking frames like this turns a long stretch of movement into a single picture. Paranal's sky, in the arid north of Chile, is a favourite with ESO's Photo Ambassadors, who keep trying out new techniques to capture more striking views of the landscape and the observatory's state-of-the-art facilities.
The VLT is ESO's flagship facility. ESO counts it among the most productive telescopes in the world and describes it as the most advanced optical instrument ever made.

understand.summary: This is a composite of many long-exposure photographs by Gianluca Lombardi; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: An observer would see sharp stars and slowly moving telescopes; combining long exposures smears both into trails and flickers.

alt: Streaked star trails flowing over large telescope enclosures and smaller telescopes, whose movement appears as blurred flickers.

caption: Sunset and moonset over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Soon after sunset, the last light of day glows as an orange haze over ESO's Paranal Observatory, coloured as it passes through the dusty lower atmosphere. Toward the lower left, a crescent Moon slowly sets, seeming to sink into the Pacific Ocean, while star trails cross the darkening sky.

This is a long-exposure composite. The trails look a bit like dotted lines because several separate shots, with short gaps between them, were combined. They bend at the bottom where the camera shifted out of place. The Moon, by contrast, is not trailed, because it was captured with a series of very short exposures.
Other visitors crossed the scene too. A meteor appears as a vertical streak in the centre, and the blinking lights of planes track horizontally across the sky.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Gabriel Brammer took the picture while working as an astronomer at the La Silla-Paranal Observatory. It was one of his very first night shots of Paranal and is still among his favourites. He later moved to the Space Telescope Science Institute in Maryland, USA, to support the Hubble Space Telescope.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based composite of several long exposures for the star trails and a series of very short exposures for the Moon, by Gabriel Brammer; the packet does not publish colour-processing details.
understand.eye: An observer would see stars as points and the Moon as a single crescent; the combined exposures turn the stars into dotted trails and the Moon into a sequence along its path.

alt: An observatory on a mountain under an orange sunset haze, with dotted star trails, a setting crescent Moon at lower left, a vertical meteor streak and horizontal plane lights.

caption: Star circles over the road to ALMA, Chile
story: Stars trace circles around the southern celestial pole, which sits at the centre of this image. Above the pole float the Magellanic Clouds, Small and Large, a pair of Milky Way satellite galaxies that can only be seen from the southern hemisphere, showing as diffuse bluish clouds. On the left, a dense crowd of stars marks the centre of the Milky Way.

ESO Photo Ambassador Adhemar Duro took the picture after pulling over at the side of the road on his way to one of ESO's observing sites in Chile. That road climbs to the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), which sits at an altitude of 5000 metres.
The circles are a product of the long exposure. As Earth turns, every star appears to orbit the celestial pole, and while the shutter stays open, each one draws an arc of light.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure photograph by Adhemar Duro; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points; the circles exist only because the long exposure recorded the sky's apparent rotation.

alt: Circular star trails centred in the frame, with two diffuse bluish clouds above the centre and a dense star field at left.

caption: A fish-eye view of the night sky at Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: This fish-eye view takes in the night sky above ESO's Astronomical Site Monitor on Cerro Armazones, a mountain in the Chilean desert near Paranal Observatory, where the Very Large Telescope (VLT) is based. A fish-eye lens squeezes an extremely wide field of view into a single frame.

Instruments like a site monitor are used to keep track of observing conditions at a location. Choosing where to put a major telescope depends on this kind of measurement, and Cerro Armazones was ultimately picked to host the planned European Extremely Large Telescope (E-ELT).

With a mirror in the 40-metre class, the E-ELT was expected to become the world's biggest eye on the sky. The quiet mountaintop in this picture was chosen to be its home, close to its neighbour the VLT at Paranal.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based fish-eye photograph credited to ESO; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A fish-eye lens takes in far more of the sky at once than the eye can, bending the view into one frame.

alt: A fish-eye view of the night sky over a desert mountaintop site.

caption: Star trails over cacti in the Atacama Desert, Chile
story: Star trails circle the South Celestial Pole above a still landscape dotted with cacti in Chile's Atacama Desert. The trails record the stars' apparent paths as Earth slowly turns, built up through long exposures.

Over the trails, a final, deeper exposure was laid on top. It brings out a host of fainter stars and, low on the horizon, the rising southern Milky Way, mottled with dark dust and marked by the familiar pink glow of the Carina Nebula.

Toward the right are the Milky Way's satellite galaxies: the Large Magellanic Cloud near the top centre and the Small Magellanic Cloud at the bottom right. Combining trails with one deep frame lets the picture show both the motion of the sky and faint detail that the trails alone would smear out.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based composite by B. Tafreshi: long exposures for the star trails, with a final deeper exposure superimposed; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees neither the trails nor so many faint stars; both come from the camera recording light over long exposures.

alt: Circular star trails over a desert landscape with cacti, with the Milky Way and a pink glow rising at the horizon and two fuzzy patches toward the right.

caption: The Milky Way over the Atacama Desert from Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: This panorama of the Atacama Desert frames a sweeping view of our Milky Way, seen with remarkable clarity because this remote area has minimal light pollution. Huge interstellar dust clouds block the light of more distant stars, giving the band its characteristic mottled look.

ESO photo ambassador Petr Horálek captured the scene in 2019 from the top of Cerro Armazones, where the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) is being built. The mountain rises to 3046 metres in the heart of the Atacama, and its height and dryness will be vital for putting the ELT's observing power to full use.
Picking a site for a new telescope is done with great care, so that it offers the best possible observing conditions. Views like this one show what Cerro Armazones has to offer.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based panoramic photograph by Petr Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A panorama takes in more of the sky than the eye can at once, and a camera gathering light over time may show the Milky Way's dust more clearly too.

alt: A wide panorama of desert under the Milky Way, whose bright band is broken by dark dust clouds.

caption: The Milky Way arching over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way arches above ESO's La Silla Observatory in this ultra high definition panorama by ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek. Our galaxy's cloudy, dusty structure forms a brilliant, glowing crown over the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, whose open dome seems to be swallowing the bright smudge of the Large Magellanic Cloud.

In the central and upper parts of the image, clouds and nebulae stand out against the dark sky in pinkish hues, among them the well-known Gum Nebula. Horálek's camera also picked up airglow in several colours, spread across the sky and near the horizon.

La Silla lies at the southern edge of the Atacama Desert, 2400 metres above sea level. From there, its many telescopes take advantage of exceptional atmospheric conditions and one of the darkest night skies on Earth to study the cosmos in fine detail.

understand.summary: This is an ultra high definition ground-based panorama by Petr Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Airglow and the pink nebulae are faint, and a camera gathering light over time reveals their colours far more readily than the eye.

alt: The Milky Way arching over an open telescope dome, with a bright smudge near the dome, pinkish nebulae higher up and coloured airglow near the horizon.

caption: The Extremely Large Telescope under construction beneath the stars, Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: Under a star-filled sky, ESO's Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) sits on top of Cerro Armazones in Chile, like a ship riding the crest of a huge, shadowy wave. Its dome is illuminated, and a thin white line above it is one of the cranes around the construction site.

It's an unusual angle on the telescope. The photographer stood at the Rolf Chini Cerro Murphy Observatory, a neighbouring facility that ESO's Paranal Observatory hosts. Look closely and you may spot the familiar cranes that surround the building work.

The ELT is due to be finished at the end of the decade. Then it will start probing this sea of stars, which ESO counts among the most pristine skies on the planet, above a desert with a rich and important heritage of skywatching.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to P. Romaniuk/ESO; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the star field may look richer here than it would to an observer at Cerro Murphy.

alt: A lit telescope dome on a dark mountain under a starry sky, with a thin white crane line above it.

caption: Star trails over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Through a night at ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), the stars appear to wheel around the southern celestial pole. On the right, one of the observatory's four 8.2-metre telescopes goes about its nightly job of studying the heavens, and two of the four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes also appear in the frame.

The observatory stands on Cerro Paranal in Chile's dry Atacama Desert, 2600 metres above sea level, and its skies give the astronomers below splendid chances to observe. That high, dry setting, together with extraordinarily advanced equipment, makes time on the VLT highly prized by astronomers around the world.
The circular paths are an effect of Earth's rotation: the stars only appear to move because our planet turns, and a camera recording over time turns that motion into trails.

understand.summary: This is a star-trail photograph by Iztok Bončina, recording the sky's apparent motion over time; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points; the trails build up only because the camera recorded Earth's rotation.

alt: Star trails circling above a large telescope enclosure on the right and two smaller round domes.

caption: The Coalsack Nebula and the Magellanic Clouds over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Two of the Very Large Telescope's Unit Telescopes sit quietly on Cerro Paranal, bathed in starlight, as the Milky Way arches over ESO's Paranal Observatory. Between the two telescopes shine the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds. Above the telescope on the left, a dark smudge lies across the Milky Way like a giant cosmic thumbprint: the Coalsack Nebula.

The Magellanic Clouds belong to the Local Group, the family of galaxies that includes our own; the Large Cloud lies 163 000 light-years from the Milky Way and the Small Cloud 200 000 light-years. The Coalsack is practically next door by comparison, roughly 600 light-years from the Solar System, and no other dark nebula is as easy to see in our skies.

Many ancient cultures recorded it. To several indigenous Australian groups it forms the head of the Emu in the Sky. Aboriginal Australians are probably the oldest astronomers in the world, and they define constellations using dark nebulae rather than stars, unlike the Western tradition.
explore: Such dark clouds stand out more in the southern sky than in the north, and other cultures drew dark constellations too. For Inca astronomers, an especially important one was Urcuchillay, the Llama, reflecting how much the animals mattered as a source of food, wool and transport. ESO photo ambassador Yuri Beletsky took the picture.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Yuri Beletsky; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The Coalsack is dark to eye and camera alike, but a camera gathering light over time may show the surrounding Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds more brightly than an observer would see them.

caption: The Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The arc of the Milky Way dominates this panorama over ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), its bright band laced with dark filaments of dust that absorb and hide the light of stars behind them, and dotted with bright patches where new stars are forming. Just below the arc hang the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, two small galactic neighbours, above two of the VLT's 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes.

On the right, beyond the row of four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes that make up the VLT, faint red and green airglow lights the sky above the horizon. Zodiacal light adds its own diffuse glow, produced by microscopic grains of dust scattering light in the plane of the Solar System.

The VLT sits 2635 metres above sea level at Paranal Observatory in northern Chile. Pictures like this, taken by ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek, show why telescopes are placed in such remote spots, and how richly the long trip there is rewarded.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based panoramic photograph by Petr Horálek; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Airglow and zodiacal light are faint, and a camera gathering light over time may show their colours and glow more clearly than the eye.

alt: The Milky Way arching over a line of four large telescope enclosures and two small domes, with two fuzzy patches below the arc and faint red and green glows near the horizon.

caption: Mars over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A calm night settles over ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert. The eye goes first to a bright reddish point left of centre in the sky: the planet Mars. On the hill to the right, ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) stands in silhouette against the stars.
Along the hilltop you can pick out the domes of the VLT's four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes and, at the right edge, the smaller VLT Survey Telescope.

In a sense, Mars appears in this picture twice. The desert around Paranal looks uncannily like the Martian surface, and the European Space Agency occasionally brings prototype rovers here to rehearse missions in realistic conditions. The red planet overhead and its earthly stand-in below make a neat pairing, which is what the picture's title, Mars near and far, plays on.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Farid Char; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Mars would look like a bright reddish point to the eye as well; the camera may also record many fainter stars than an observer would notice.

alt: A bright reddish point in a starry sky above a hill topped with silhouetted telescope domes.

caption: The Galactic Centre above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla is at work, its dome lit by the Moon. Across the frame runs the Milky Way, our galaxy, a disc seen perfectly edge-on. Above the dome, partly hidden by dark dust clouds, bulges the galaxy's prominent yellowish centre.

The galactic plane holds a hundred thousand million stars along with a great deal of interstellar gas and dust. The dust absorbs visible light and re-emits it at longer wavelengths, so to our eyes it looks completely opaque. Ancient Andean civilisations saw animal-shaped constellations in these dark lanes. Follow the lane that seems to grow upward from the galactic centre and you arrive at Antares (Alpha Scorpii) and the reddish nebula surrounding it.

The Galactic Centre sits in Sagittarius and is best seen during the southern winter. The telescope, inaugurated in 1976, now works with the HARPS spectrograph, which ESO calls the world's most precise exoplanet hunter.
explore: La Silla lies on the outskirts of the Chilean Atacama Desert, 600 km north of Santiago and 2400 m above sea level. It was ESO's first site in Chile and was the largest observatory of its time. ESO Photo Ambassador Serge Brunier took this photograph.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Serge Brunier; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The dust lanes are opaque to the eye in visible light, and a camera gathering light over time may show the yellowish bulge and the reddish nebula more vividly than an observer would see them.

alt: The Milky Way running edge-on across the sky, with its yellowish central bulge partly hidden by dark dust above a moonlit telescope dome.

caption: The Milky Way over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The glowing plane of the Milky Way, seen edge-on and laced with bands of dust and dark gas, slices across the night sky above ESO's facilities on Mount Paranal in Chile's Atacama Desert. In the lower right corner hangs the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of our galaxy's satellites, above the Residencia, where staff and visitors stay.

The three-minute exposure also caught some action on the ground. At left, a car pauses, parking lights glowing, to drop off a passenger. Even under the Milky Way's glow the high desert stays quite dark, so the passenger carries a small flashlight along the path to the Residencia's underground entrance ramp; its light traces a bright squiggle. At lower right, the Residencia's rooftop glass dome mirrors the starry sky.
Paranal hosts the Very Large Telescope (VLT), which ESO describes as the world's most advanced ground-based astronomical observatory.
explore: When this picture was published, two new survey telescopes were being built at Paranal: VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, and the VLT Survey Telescope (VST). Both were expected to begin work in the 2009-2010 timeframe.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph taken with a digital camera and a three-minute exposure, credited to B. Fugate (FASORtronics)/ESO; the packet does not publish colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Three minutes of exposure gathers far more light than the eye, which is why the Milky Way looks so bright here while the desert actually stayed quite dark, and why the moving flashlight became a squiggly line.

alt: The Milky Way slicing across a dark sky over desert buildings, with a vehicle's lights at left, a squiggly flashlight trail, a glass dome reflecting stars and a fuzzy patch at lower right.

caption: Dotted star trails over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Dotted trails of starlight curve around the southern celestial pole above ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT). Its four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes dominate the scene, their movements turned into a seemingly frantic blur as they swung between targets through the night. One of the smaller Auxiliary Telescopes hides in the bottom left corner.

The picture combines 450 exposures of 20 seconds each, covering two and a half hours of apparent stellar motion. That motion is an illusion: it is Earth, not the stars, that turns as time passes. One frame even caught a shooting star, a small streak above the Auxiliary Telescope.

The sky over Cerro Paranal, 2600 metres up in Chile's Atacama Desert, is so dark and clear that long photo sequences like this can be made without a single cloud getting in the way. The image is the work of Farid Char, a student at Chile's Universidad Católica del Norte.

understand.eye: An observer would see sharp stars and slowly turning telescopes; combining the sequence turns the stars into dotted trails and the telescopes' motion into a blur.

caption: Gegenschein and the Milky Way over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: On the right of this image, the arc of the Milky Way soars above ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, an observatory ESO is a partner in. On the arc to the left, however, a different glow competes for attention: a faint brightening of the night sky.

That glow is gegenschein, German for "countershine". It sits along the ecliptic at the point directly opposite the Sun, and it arises when interplanetary dust in the outer Solar System, shed by comets and broken-up asteroids, scatters incoming sunlight.

Across most of the world, light pollution from artificial sources hides sights such as gegenschein and even the Milky Way. By some estimates, more than 80% of the world's population lives under light-polluted skies, which makes places like the Atacama Desert, home to ALMA, all the more special.

caption: A stargazer beneath the Milky Way at the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: On the right of the frame, a stargazer points up at the arc of the Milky Way curving overhead at ESO's Paranal Observatory. Across the left are the telescopes of the Very Large Telescope (VLT): all four boxy Unit Telescopes plus three of the rounder Auxiliary Telescopes, of which there are four. The pointing figure is ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi.

Tafreshi was one of four leading astrophotographers and videographers who travelled to Paranal in 2016 for ESO's UHD Expedition. Over a few weeks they gathered ultra high definition stills, fulldome timelapses, 360-degree panoramas and plenty of striking views of their surroundings, all aimed at planetarium shows.

The results are used by the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Centre. ESO runs the centre jointly with the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies, in a building donated by the German foundation Klaus Tschira Stiftung.

caption: A 360-degree panorama of the Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: At first glance this ultra high definition panorama of ESO's Paranal Observatory, home of the Very Large Telescope (VLT), looks strange. The Milky Way seems to plunge through the night sky as two separate columns, while still filling the sky along the top of the frame.

The distortion comes from how ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek made the image. He photographed the whole dome of the sky, from the zenith down to the horizon, all 360 degrees around. The two apparent Milky Ways are really one band: the plane of our galaxy arching across the sky from one horizon to the other.

Where the band passes overhead, it gets stretched along the top edge of the panorama. That is the price of squeezing the entire dome of the sky into a flat rectangle, much as flat world maps stretch the regions near the poles. In reality, the Milky Way graces the skies above Paranal every night, in striking detail and clarity.

understand.summary: This is a 360-degree ultra high definition panorama by Petr Horálek, covering the sky from zenith to horizon and flattened into a rectangle; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: An observer would see a single band of the Milky Way arching overhead; the two columns are a product of flattening the whole sky into one image.

caption: A 360-degree panorama of the Milky Way over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: It is another clear night at ESO's Paranal Observatory, and our galaxy, the Milky Way, arcs across the sky in this 360-degree panorama by ESO Photo Ambassador Gabriel Brammer. The panorama wraps the full circle of the horizon into a single frame. Toward the right, a visiting astronomer stands admiring the view.

For many city dwellers, surrounded by crowds and artificial light, a view of our cosmic home this detailed is no longer possible. A clear night like this one is perfect for sitting back and simply taking it in.

Today we know this band is our home galaxy, but the Ancient Greeks saw the hand of the gods in it. In their legends, the cloudy streak was the breast milk of Hera, wife of Zeus. We also owe them the name: the Hellenistic phrase galaxias kyklos means "milky circle" and is the root of our modern name.

understand.summary: This is a 360-degree ground-based panorama by Gabriel Brammer; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: No eye takes in a full circle of sky at once, and a camera gathering light over time may also show the Milky Way more brightly than the watching astronomer sees it.

caption: Antu, and Yepun's lasers beneath the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Against a dark sky, Unit Telescope 1, known as Antu, takes centre stage at ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT). Behind it hides a near-identical twin, UT4 or Yepun, sending its laser beams up toward the stars, while the Milky Way stretches low along the horizon. Chilean astrophotographer Alexis Trigo captured the scene.
The VLT has four Unit Telescopes, each with a mirror 8.2 m across and a dome as big as a family house that shields it from the elements. Yepun stands apart as the only one carrying four lasers.

The lasers make artificial stars in Earth's upper atmosphere, letting astronomers measure and correct the turbulence that blurs their data. At first only UT4 had lasers. That changed recently when the VLT Interferometer's GRAVITY+ upgrade was completed, adding a laser to each of the other three. Even so, Yepun's set of four keeps it distinctive.

understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the laser beams and the Milky Way may look brighter here than to someone standing nearby.

caption: The Magellanic Clouds over the Atacama Desert coast, Chile
story: From right to left across this sky are the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds, two irregular galaxies that neighbour the Milky Way. On the left horizon, a real cloud leans into view.

Magellan's expedition was the first to report these objects, at the beginning of the XVI century. At the time, they were taken for thin clouds that were oddly motionless. Real clouds are common here: humidity from the cold Pacific Ocean, together with the temperature contrast with the ground, often blankets the Atacama Desert's shoreline. That moisture feeds the local plants, many kinds of cacti, a lot of them found nowhere else.

The cold ocean also keeps the so-called inversion layer very low, leaving the air above the clouds exceptionally dry and clear. Those are the conditions at Paranal Observatory, 2600 metres up and only 12 km from the coast. It is home to ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), which ESO calls the most advanced optical ground-based telescope in the world.

understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Magellanic Clouds may look brighter and more defined here than to someone on the coast.

alt: Two fuzzy patches, the Magellanic Clouds, in a starry sky above the desert coast, with a cloud rising from the left horizon.

caption: A laser guide star launched from Yepun under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A powerful laser beam leaps from Yepun, one of the 8.2-metre telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT). Across the top of the image stretches the Milky Way, seen perfectly edge-on, with the galaxy's yellowish central bulge crossed by prominent dark lanes.

High in Earth's mesosphere, the beam excites sodium atoms, making an artificial star 90 km up. Known as the Laser Guide Star, it belongs to the VLT's adaptive optics system, which lets astronomers correct their images and spectra for the blurring caused by the atmosphere.

Those dark lanes are vast clouds of interstellar dust, impenetrable to visible light. Ancient Andean civilisations saw constellations in these dark nebulae, shaped like familiar animals; one of them, the llama, is visible on the right. The VLT itself is made up of four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes, of which Yepun is UT4, plus four movable Auxiliary Telescopes, each 1.8 metres across.

understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the laser beam and the Milky Way's bulge may look brighter here than to an observer on the platform.

caption: Green airglow over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: A magical green glow fills the sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory, on the outskirts of Chile's Atacama Desert. From left to right below it stand the 3.6m telescope and New Technology Telescope, both ESO's, then the Swiss 1.2-metre Leonhard Euler Telescope.

The glow is airglow, faint light given off by Earth's atmosphere. It is invisible to the naked eye, but sensitive cameras can record it in very dark places with little light pollution, like this one. Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun sets off chemical processes that make atoms in the upper atmosphere shine very weakly. Here the green comes from oxygen atoms; other atoms or molecules can make it red or yellow.

Airglow should not be mistaken for an aurora. Auroras are fleeting, dancing displays caused by charged particles flung into Earth's magnetic field, while airglow is always there, more like quiet background music.
explore: The telescopes can be visited in person. Tours take place during the day so they do not disturb the night's work, which means no airglow, but ESO says the telescopes more than make up for it.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph by J. Pérez taken with a sensitive camera; the packet does not publish exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Airglow is invisible to the naked eye; only a sensitive camera picks up its green light.

caption: A laser guide star aimed at the Milky Way's centre, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A laser beam from Yepun, an 8.2-metre telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), points straight at the centre of our galaxy, right into the heart of the Milky Way's brightest region. The galactic plane is crossed by prominent dark lanes, vast clouds of interstellar dust that block visible light.
The beam belongs to the VLT's adaptive optics system, making an artificial star 90 km up in Earth's mesosphere, which serves as a reference for correcting images and spectra for atmospheric blurring.

Although dust hides the galactic core from visible light, Yepun carries infrared instruments that can see through it. With them, astronomers study the complex, turbulent centre of the Milky Way, where a supermassive black hole lurks. The VLT consists of four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes, of which Yepun is UT4, and four movable Auxiliary Telescopes of 1.8 metres.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based visible-light photograph by G. Hüdepohl; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Like this photograph, the eye cannot see through the dust lanes; only infrared instruments such as those on Yepun can peer into the galactic core.

alt: A laser beam rising toward the brightest part of the Milky Way, which is crossed by dark lanes of dust.

caption: The Galactic Centre above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Lit by moonlight, the dome of the ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla is at work on a night of observations. Overhead, the Milky Way crosses the whole picture as a disc viewed exactly edge-on, and above the dome its yellowish central bulge shines out, partly veiled by dark clouds of dust.

Our galaxy's plane contains a hundred thousand million stars and plenty of interstellar gas and dust. That dust soaks up visible light and gives it off again at longer wavelengths, so to the eye it is completely opaque. In these dark lanes, ancient Andean peoples traced constellations shaped like animals. Trace the lane that climbs from the galactic centre toward the top of the frame and you come to a reddish nebula surrounding Antares, also called Alpha Scorpii.

The Galactic Centre is in the constellation Sagittarius and is best placed for viewing during the southern winter. The telescope beneath it opened in 1976 and today operates the HARPS spectrograph, which ESO calls the world's most precise exoplanet hunter.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Alexandre Santerne took this photograph. La Silla, 600 km north of Santiago and 2400 m up on the edge of the Chilean Atacama Desert, was ESO's first site in Chile and in its day the largest observatory anywhere.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by Alexandre Santerne; the packet does not publish camera, exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: The dust lanes are opaque to the eye in visible light, and a camera gathering light over time may show the bulge and the reddish nebula more vividly than an observer would.

alt: The Milky Way crossing the sky edge-on, with its yellowish bulge partly hidden by dark dust above a moonlit telescope dome.

caption: Twilight and star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The last rays of sunlight paint a blend of orange, red and yellow near the horizon at ESO's La Silla Observatory, but the bright star trails curving through the sky steal the show. Each trail marks the path of a single star, recorded over a long exposure. Below, the rear lights of moving vehicles leave their own trails, tracing the region's network of roads.

ESO Photo Ambassador Roger Wesson made the picture by combining 763 separate 20-second exposures. He began approximately 40 minutes after sunset and kept going through the night, so that both the fading twilight and the lengthening star trails appear in one image.
Sunset is when the observatory's staff can get down to their real work: studying and exploring the night sky. ESO's first observatory, La Silla remains among the most productive in the world.

understand.summary: This is a composite of 763 exposures of 20 seconds each by Roger Wesson, spanning twilight and the night; the packet does not publish camera or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: No observer could see twilight and hours of star motion at once; the combined exposures place them together in a single frame.

alt: Curving star trails over an observatory, with orange, red and yellow twilight at the horizon and vehicle light trails along roads below.

caption: The Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: This view from ESO's Paranal Observatory shows the Milky Way above the Very Large Telescope (VLT), with three of its four Unit Telescopes in the frame. The photograph, credited to P. Horálek/ESO, carries the title Colourful skies over Paranal Observatory.

The VLT's Unit Telescopes can work together as a giant interferometer. Combining their light in this way lets astronomers see much finer detail than any one telescope could. ESO describes the VLT as the world's most advanced optical instrument.

The Milky Way looks richly detailed here, yet a single VLT telescope can pick out objects some four billion times fainter than the unaided eye can see. That power has opened a new age of discoveries, and the VLT has notched up several notable scientific firsts, among them the first image of a planet outside our Solar System.

understand.eye: A camera gathering light over time shows more of the Milky Way than the eye, though a single VLT telescope reaches objects four billion times fainter than the unaided eye can see.

caption: The Milky Way arching over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Just right of centre in this panorama, the four Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) pose in front of a vast expanse of the Milky Way, which arches over the site almost like a rainbow made of stars.

The four smaller Auxiliary Telescopes are in the picture too, and spotting them is a small challenge for the viewer. They can be moved around on tracks across the telescope platform, so astronomers can arrange them in different configurations to suit their observations.

The photograph was taken at ESO's Paranal Observatory, which sits proudly on top of Cerro Paranal, 2635 metres high, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Credited to ESO/P. Horálek, the panorama sets the telescopes against the very sky they are built to explore.

caption: The Milky Way above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: During a night of observing at La Silla, the moonlit dome of the ESO 3.6-metre telescope sits beneath the Milky Way, which spans the picture as a disc-shaped galaxy seen precisely edge-on. The bright, prominent bulge at its centre rises above the dome, partly screened by dark dust clouds.

The galaxy's plane is home to a hundred thousand million stars, mixed with a considerable amount of interstellar gas and dust. The dust absorbs visible light and re-radiates it at longer wavelengths, which is why these lanes look utterly dark to our eyes. Long ago, Andean civilisations read animal figures into them. One dark lane appears to rise from the centre toward the top of the image; following it leads to the reddish nebula around the star Antares (Alpha Scorpii).

The Galactic Centre lies in Sagittarius and is best seen in the southern winter. Inaugurated in 1976, the telescope now works with HARPS, a spectrograph ESO describes as the most precise exoplanet hunter in the world.
explore: The photograph is by ESO Photo Ambassador Alexandre Santerne. La Silla, ESO's first site in Chile, lies 600 km north of Santiago at an altitude of 2400 m, on the fringes of the Atacama Desert, and was the largest observatory of its time.

caption: Centaurus over the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The constellation of Centaurus hangs above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert, set among the crowded stars of the Milky Way. The two bright stars just above the dome are Alpha and Beta Centauri.

Centaurus also contains Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf that is our nearest stellar neighbour. It was the focus of the Pale Red Dot campaign, an international hunt for an Earth-like planet orbiting this nearest of stars that combined science with public outreach.

The search was set to use HARPS, attached to the 3.6-metre telescope seen here, along with BOOTES (the Burst Optical Observer and Transient Exploring System) and the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Telescope Network (LCOGT). The public would be able to watch teams of astronomers with different specialities gather, analyse and interpret data that might, or might not, confirm such a planet.

caption: The Milky Way over the Astronomical Site Monitor on Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: At night on Cerro Armazones in Chile's Atacama Desert, the Milky Way stretches across the sky above ESO's Astronomical Site Monitor. Our galaxy's disc is seen edge-on, and to the left of the tall tower its centre appears as a yellow bulge scored with dark lanes.

Those dark lanes are nebulae, where cosmic dust blocks the light behind. In ancient Andean cosmology they formed constellations of their own. One of them, the llama, extends rightward from a point above the tower; its eye is the bright star Alpha Centauri.

Cerro Armazones lies about 20 km from Cerro Paranal and ESO's Very Large Telescope, and it is the chosen site for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). Monitoring equipment like the one pictured helps characterise the conditions a site offers. ESO Photo Ambassador Serge Brunier took this photograph.

caption: An Auxiliary Telescope and the setting Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Seen from the platform of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) on Paranal, a magnificent Milky Way sets very low over the horizon, with one of the observatory's Auxiliary Telescopes in the foreground. The galaxy's core shows as a yellowish bulge scored with dark dust lanes, and the brightest dot above it is Jupiter.

Catching the Milky Way this low is possible thanks to the exceptional quality of Paranal's sky. Near the horizon, starlight passes through much more air, so only a very clear, dark sky shows the band so well.

The VLT has four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes and four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes. The Auxiliary Telescopes are dedicated to interferometry, a technique that lets astronomers see details up to 25 times finer than the individual telescopes can. Running on rails, they can be moved across the platform to 30 different positions.

caption: A laser guide star and star trails over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Under a dark, clear sky streaked with star trails, a laser beam leaps upward from Yepun, the fourth of the Unit Telescopes making up ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT). The VLT is ESO's flagship facility, sited at Paranal Observatory in northern Chile's Atacama Desert.

The beam creates an artificial star above Paranal to help the VLT's adaptive optics instruments. The system watches how that artificial star is distorted and corrects for it. In this way adaptive optics lets astronomers overcome the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere, producing images almost as sharp as they would be if the entire telescope were out in space.
The star trails, meanwhile, record the passage of time. As Earth turns, the stars appear to sweep across the sky, and a long exposure stretches each one into an arc.

caption: The Milky Way at dawn over the Paranal Residencia, Chile
story: Looking south from the Paranal Residencia just as the first light of dawn touches the horizon, the Milky Way fills the left side of the picture. Within it, the dark Coal Sack nebula and the reddish Carina Nebula are easy to pick out. Toward the right edge, the Large Magellanic Cloud is visible too.
At the bottom of the frame sits a white dome 35 metres across. It is the only visible part of the Paranal Residencia, a building that is otherwise almost entirely hidden from view.

The Residencia is light-insulated so that no artificial light escapes during the night, when the observatory's telescopes are at work. Its dome is covered by an umbrella-shaped blackout curtain that closes automatically at sunset and opens again at sunrise.

caption: Comet Lovejoy, the Moon and a laser over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Night has fallen over ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert. Comet Lovejoy hangs low on the horizon, just right of the Moon. One of the giant Unit Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope (VLT) fires a reddish laser beam upward, and above it a satellite has left a streak across the sky.

The laser creates an artificial star that helps astronomers make sharper observations. ESO describes the VLT as the world's most advanced visible-light astronomical observatory. The photograph was taken on 22 December 2011.

Cerro Paranal is a mountain 2600 metres high, about 130 km south of Antofagasta and 12 km from the Pacific coast, in one of the world's driest regions. The clear view of the Milky Way's stars here shows how good its observing conditions are.

caption: Centaurus over the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Stars of the constellation Centaurus spread across the sky above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope in this view from La Silla Observatory, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile.

Centaurus holds Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf and our closest stellar neighbour. When this picture was released, Proxima was the target of a new science and outreach project called the Pale Red Dot campaign, an international effort to find out whether an Earth-like planet orbits the nearest star to us.

The campaign planned to use HARPS, the instrument on the 3.6-metre telescope pictured here, together with the LCOGT telescope network and the BOOTES system. It also set out to let the public follow along as astronomers with different skills pooled their efforts to gather, analyse and interpret data that might or might not reveal such a planet.
explore: Updates from the campaign were planned as blog posts and social media messages on the Pale Red Dot Twitter account, under the hashtag #PaleRedDot, and on the campaign's own website.

caption: The VLT Survey Telescope under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: In this high-resolution panorama of ESO's Paranal Observatory, the VLT Survey Telescope (VST) and its dome hold centre stage in the foreground, beneath the Milky Way's arc. Many nebulae are scattered along our galaxy's arc and the area around the constellation Orion, at lower right.

Above the VLT Unit Telescope glows the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the Milky Way's satellite galaxies. Although the Atacama sky is usually dark, faint, colourful airglow often brightens it, particularly close to the horizon.

ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek took the image on 4 April 2016. The picture's title, A Dark Sky Full of Light, sums up the scene: a sky that is typically dark, yet here is crowded with glowing nebulae, galaxies and airglow.

caption: The Milky Way over snow-covered trees, Torres del Paine National Park, Chile
story: Snow-covered trees stand beneath a magnificent night sky in Torres del Paine National Park, in Southern Patagonia, Chile's XII Region. It is a long way from the desert observatories of the north, in a landscape of snow rather than sand. The two brightest stars in the prominent band of the Milky Way are Alpha Centauri, above, and Beta Centauri, below.

A little lower on the right sits the globular cluster Omega Centauri. On the left, above the trees, are the Small Magellanic Cloud and the globular cluster 47 Tucanae. A globular cluster is a dense ball of old stars held together by gravity.

Chile's desert skies are renowned for their clarity, but this picture shows that the rest of this long country can offer phenomenal stargazing too. Here, far to the south, snow and a clear night combine in a different kind of astronomical landscape.

caption: The Milky Way at twilight over the Atacama Desert, Chile
story: The Milky Way emerges at twilight over the Atacama Desert. Directly over the rock in the middle of the frame sits the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way, and above it lies the reddish spot of the bright Carina Nebula, a glowing cloud of gas.

Further left, along the plane of the Milky Way, you can spot the Southern Cross with the Coal Sack. The Coal Sack is a dark cloud of dust that blocks the starlight behind it. Next come two bright stars, Beta and Alpha Centauri.
The Atacama Desert has hosted ESO's observatories since the 1960s, and it is the chosen site for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), which ESO calls the world's biggest eye on the sky.

caption: Star trails and the VLT's laser guide star, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: On a dark, clear night, stars leave trails across the sky while, beneath them, a laser beam rises from Yepun. This is the fourth Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT), described by ESO as Europe's flagship observatory.

The laser produces an artificial star above Paranal, which supports the VLT's adaptive optics instruments. Adaptive optics counters the blurring effect of our atmosphere and can deliver images nearly as sharp as a telescope placed in space would record.

Without it, the constant churning of the air above a ground-based telescope smears fine detail, the same effect that makes stars appear to twinkle. The star trails come from Earth's rotation: over a long exposure, each star appears to sweep out an arc. The photograph is credited to Dave Jones/ESO.

caption: The Milky Way over an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A magnificent Milky Way spreads over one of the Auxiliary Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) on Cerro Paranal in Chile. The exceptional quality of the sky at this site is what makes such a view possible.

The VLT combines four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes with four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes; one of the smaller ones is in this photograph. The Auxiliary Telescopes are devoted to interferometry, which merges light from several telescopes so astronomers can make out details up to 25 times finer than any single telescope reveals.

Rails let the Auxiliary Telescopes travel across the observing platform, and they can be parked at 30 different positions. Moving them changes the way their light combines, which lets astronomers tune the array to what they are studying.

caption: Zodiacal light over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Rising from the horizon at La Silla, a roughly triangular, diffuse white glow reaches up into the night sky. This is zodiacal light, which seems to extend from the neighbourhood of the Sun along the ecliptic, the band of the zodiac.

The glow comes from sunlight scattered by dust spread between the planets in the plane of the Solar System. The Sun itself is below the horizon, but its light still reaches those dust grains and is scattered toward us.

In spring and autumn, when the zodiac rises steeply from the horizon, the best times to look are just after sunset or just before sunrise. That tilt helps lift the glow higher, out of the thick air near the ground, so it is easier to see from a dark site like this one.

caption: Cerro Armazones at night, Chile
story: This night view shows Cerro Armazones, a mountain in Chile not far from ESO's Paranal Observatory, home of the flagship Very Large Telescope. The mountain was one of the places considered for the future Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), which, with a mirror in the 40-metre class, is set to be the world's biggest eye on the sky.

The ELT programme office studied half a dozen potential sites. Sky quality was only part of the picture: the choice also weighed wider scientific factors and practical needs for building and running an observatory, such as access, water and power supplies, and political stability.

Cerro Armazones made the final short list of the ELT Site Selection Advisory Committee and was its preferred site. It offered the best balance of sky quality across all the factors considered, and it could be run in an integrated way with the existing Paranal Observatory.

caption: The Milky Way aligned with the New Technology Telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way lines up perfectly with the opening of the New Technology Telescope (NTT) at ESO's La Silla Observatory, so the telescope seems to be swallowing our galaxy.

The NTT's octagonal enclosure was a technological breakthrough in its own right. The dome is relatively small, and a system of flaps ventilates it so that air flows smoothly across the mirror. That cuts down turbulence, which would otherwise blur the view, and so produces sharper images.

Air turbulence is a constant challenge for astronomers. Pockets of air at different temperatures bend light slightly differently, so the air inside and around a dome can blur a telescope's images much as the atmosphere does. By keeping the air flowing evenly, the NTT's design keeps its view of the sky clear.

caption: The Milky Way and Comet 252P/LINEAR over the Paranal Residencia, Chile
story: Above the lit dome of the Residencia at ESO's Paranal Observatory, the Milky Way stretches in a magical arc across the sky. Toward the left, near the horizon, is Comet 252P/LINEAR.

A comet is a small icy body that develops a fuzzy glow as it nears the Sun. On 22–23 March 2016 this one made only its fifth close approach to Earth on record. Although the dome in the foreground is lit, the Residencia produces no light pollution that would hamper the work of the telescopes.

The picture comes from ESO's Fulldome Expedition to Chile, in which a team of photographers gathered spectacular images for planetarium presentations. Fulldome images are made to be projected across the curved ceiling of a planetarium, surrounding the audience with the sky.

understand.eye: A camera gathering light over time can reveal a faint comet near the horizon that the eye might easily miss.

caption: Star trails over Licancabur Volcano, Chile
story: Stars trace long trails across the sky above Licancabur Volcano in this long-exposure image. Straddling the Chile–Bolivia border, the volcano is part of the Andean Central Volcanic Zone. Volcanoes of the Andes form where one of Earth's tectonic plates slides beneath another.
Licancabur is 5916 metres high, far taller than Mont Blanc, Europe's highest mountain. The photograph is credited to S. Otarola/ESO.

The trails are not caused by the stars moving. It is Earth's rotation that shifts their positions in our sky, and a long exposure records each star's apparent path as a streak of light. Stars near the celestial pole trace tight circles, while those farther away sweep out longer arcs. The longer the exposure, the longer each trail grows.

understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points; the trails appear only because the long exposure recorded Earth's rotation.

caption: The Milky Way and bright airglow over the Atacama Desert, Chile
story: The Milky Way shines brightly overhead in this view from Chile's Atacama Desert. In the background, an orange and yellow shimmer that looks rather like an aurora adds to the quiet beauty of the sky.

The shimmer is airglow, produced by chemical reactions in the atmosphere that give off light. Usually those emissions are not very strong, but they were unusually strong on the night of this photograph, giving the picture its unusual look. A display this strong is not the norm.

The photograph was taken during the ESO Ultra HD Expedition and is credited to ESO/B. Tafreshi. Unlike an aurora, which is caused by charged particles from space, airglow comes from the atmosphere's own chemistry and is present every night, though usually too faint to notice.

understand.eye: Even unusually bright airglow is faint, and a camera gathering light over time shows its orange and yellow colours more strongly than the eye.

caption: Star trails over an ALMA antenna, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Stars seem to rain down on one of the 66 antennas that make up the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), on the Chajnantor Plateau high in the Chilean Andes. The downpour is really a long exposure recording the stars' trails across the sky as Earth rotates.

It is just as well this is not real rain. The plateau was chosen partly because it is so dry. Radio waves pass easily through Earth's atmosphere, but water vapour in the air soaks them up and degrades what astronomers can record.

Europe, North America and East Asia run ALMA together as an international partnership, working in cooperation with the Republic of Chile. The photo, taken by K. Ashitagawa, was provided by NAOJ, the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan.
